title: Joel 2:12–17
context: In 2:12 the LORD speaks: “Yet even now… turn to me with all your heart.” The prophet continues (2:13–14), calling the people to tear their hearts and not their garments, and grounding the call in the LORD’s character: “gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness,” words that echo Exodus 34:6 and reappear in Jonah 4:2. “Who knows? He may turn and relent” (2:14) closely resembles the king’s words in Jonah 3:9. The prophet then calls for a sacred assembly of everyone, from elders to nursing infants and newlyweds (2:15–16), and gives the priests a prayer: “Spare your people, LORD” (2:17). On God’s relenting, see the Jonah 3:10, Judges 10:16, and 1 Samuel 15:29 boxes; on the heart that turns, see the Deuteronomy 10:16 box. Shared ground: both traditions read the passage as a heartfelt call to repentance grounded in God’s mercy.

verses.text: “Yet even now,” says the LORD, “turn to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, Yet even now, turn to me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning. Arminian readers see a genuine invitation, offered even at the edge of judgment, that people are able to answer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the call as God’s gracious summons, through which he works the turning he commands. Shared ground: both traditions read yet even now as a word of hope.

verses.text: Tear your heart and not your garments, and turn to the LORD, your God; for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and relents from sending calamity.
verses.arminianNotes: Joel calls them to tear their hearts, not their garments, for the LORD is gracious, merciful, and relents from calamity. Arminian readers see inward repentance as the response God seeks, grounded in his compassion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the echo of Exodus 34:6 and see God’s character as the basis of hope. Both traditions read tear your heart as calling for sincere repentance over outward show; on God’s relenting, see the Jonah 3:10 and Judges 10:16 boxes.

verses.text: Who knows? He may turn and relent, and leave a blessing behind him, even a meal offering and a drink offering to the LORD, your God.
verses.arminianNotes: Who knows? He may turn and relent, and leave a blessing, even offerings for the LORD. Arminian readers see real openness in the outcome, as God responds to his people’s repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the who knows as humble hope that does not presume on God’s mercy, compare Jonah 3:9 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as hope without presumption; on relenting language, see the 1 Samuel 15:29 box.

verses.text: Blow the trumpet in Zion! Sanctify a fast. Call a solemn assembly.
verses.arminianNotes: Joel repeats the call: blow the trumpet in Zion, sanctify a fast, call a solemn assembly. Arminian readers note that the same trumpet that warned of judgment in 2:1 now summons the people to repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repetition of 1:14 stressing the urgency of corporate response. Both traditions read the verse as turning alarm into worship, with the community gathered before God.

verses.text: Gather the people. Sanctify the assembly. Assemble the elders. Gather the children, and those who nurse from breasts. Let the bridegroom go out of his room, and the bride out of her chamber.
verses.arminianNotes: Everyone is to gather, elders, children, nursing infants, even bride and groom from their chambers. Arminian readers see the whole community included, no one excused from seeking God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that even newlyweds, normally exempt from duties, are called, showing the gravity of the moment. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a picture of total communal participation in repentance.

verses.text: Let the priests, the ministers of the LORD, weep between the porch and the altar, and let them say, “Spare your people, LORD, and don’t give your heritage to reproach, that the nations should rule over them. Why should they say among the peoples, ‘Where is their God?’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The priests weep between porch and altar, praying, Spare your people, LORD, lest the nations ask, Where is their God? Arminian readers see intercession appealing to God’s compassion and reputation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prayer grounded in concern for God’s name among the nations. Both traditions read the verse as a model of intercession that pleads both God’s mercy toward his people and his honor before others.
